sections.heading: 2.1 Inference-time alignment framework
sections.text: Our framework is inspired by that of Huang et al. [13] , Huang et al. [14] , although we consider different desiderata. Throughout, we let 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} denote a space of possible responses and 𝒳 \mathcal{X} denote a space of possible prompts or contexts. A language model is any map π : 𝒳 → Δ ⁡ ( 𝒴 ) \pi:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta(\mathcal{Y}) from prompts to distributions over responses; due to the connections with RL, we use the terms language model and policy interchangeably. For the purposes of analysis, we will suppose that there exists a true reward function r ⋆ : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → ℝ r^{\star}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} that measures the quality of a response y y given a prompt x x ; in practice, this reward function will be unknown and only accessible through some learned reward model r ^ : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → ℝ \widehat{r}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} . For the sake of simplicity, we will always assume that 0 ≤ r ⋆ ​ ( x , y ) , r ^ ​ ( x , y ) ≤ R max 0\leq r^{\star}(x,y),\widehat{r}(x,y)\leq R_{\mathrm{max}} for some known R max > 0 R_{\mathrm{max}}>0 . As in Huang et al. [14] , we will consider a simplified setting where the prompt x x is fixed throughout, and thus we will suppress it from notation for clarity, i.e., we will write π ref ​ ( ⋅ ) \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot) instead of π ref ( ⋅ | x ) \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x) and similarly for r ⋆ r^{\star} and r ^ \widehat{r} . Note that there is no loss of generality in doing so, as we can take expectations over the marginal distribution of prompts at the end of our analysis if desired. We suppose that the learner has access to the following computational model, motivated by the fact that empirical LM inference engines like vLLM [ 18 ] can quickly sample from large language models and evaluate reward models in parallel.

sections.heading: Definition 1 (Sample-and-Evaluate) .
sections.text: The learner has access to a reference model π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} from which he can sample responses y ∼ π ref y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} independently. In addition, for any sampled response y y , the learner can query the reward model r ^ \widehat{r} to obtain the reward value r ^ ​ ( y ) \widehat{r}(y) . The efficiency of the learner is measured by the total number of samples, N N , drawn from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} . The goal of the learner is to use this sample-and-evaluate access to produce a response y ^ \hat{y} that achieves high true reward r ⋆ ​ ( y ^ ) r^{\star}(\hat{y}) while using as few samples from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} as possible. In order to evaluate candidate policies π ^ \widehat{\pi} producing responses y ^ ∼ π ^ \hat{y}\sim\widehat{\pi} , it is natural to compare them to some comparator policy π ⋆ \pi^{\star} that achieves high true reward through regret. While Huang et al. [14] consider regret in terms of expected true reward, i.e., trying to minimize 𝔼 y ∼ π ⋆ ​ [ r ⋆ ​ ( y ) ] − 𝔼 y ∼ π ^ ​ [ r ⋆ ​ ( y ) ] \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{\star}}[r^{\star}(y)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\widehat{\pi}}[r^{\star}(y)] , we note that in many practical settings, the true reward is either (i) binary or (ii) accessible only through (potentially noisy) pairwise comparisons. In the former case, expected true reward drastically simplifies to a search problem and is tightly analyzed in Huang et al. [14] . In the latter case, however, the expected numerical value of the reward is less meaningful as the learner will never have access to r ⋆ r^{\star} itself. Instead, we consider the win-rate induced by r ⋆ r^{\star} of the learned policy against the comparator policy π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , defined to be: R r ⋆ ​ ( π ) = ℙ y ∼ π , y ′ ∼ π ref ​ ( r ⋆ ​ ( y ) > r ⋆ ​ ( y ′ ) ) + 1 2 ⋅ ℙ y ∼ π , y ′ ∼ π ref ​ ( r ⋆ ​ ( y ) = r ⋆ ​ ( y ′ ) ) . \displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi)=\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(r^{\star}(y)>r^{\star}(y^{\prime}))+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\pi,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left(r^{\star}(y)=r^{\star}(y^{\prime})\right). (2) More generally, r ⋆ r^{\star} could be replaced with another reward function, such as r ^ \widehat{r} , and ( 2 ) would define the win-rate under that reward function. We remark that while ( 2 ) uses the base model from which we draw candidate samples, π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , as the comparator policy, in principle one could evaluate win-rate against an arbitrary comparison distribution q q . This latter setting is relevant in practice, as it corresponds to AlpacaEval-style pipelines [ 8 , 7 ] where q q corresponds to a strong comparator like GPT-4. For the sake of simplicity and clarity of presentation, we will first present our results for the special case where q = π ref q=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , and then show that for general q q , under natural closeness assumptions between q q and π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , the same arguments yield qualitatively similar results, which we detail in Section 6 . It is immediate that expected rewards coincide (up to a constant factor) with the notion of win rate in the special case where all reward functions are binary. Given a comparator policy π ⋆ \pi^{\star} , we wish to minimize the regret of a candidate policy π ^ \widehat{\pi} , i.e., Reg ⁡ ( π ^ ) = R r ⋆ ​ ( π ⋆ ) − R r ⋆ ​ ( π ^ ) \reg(\widehat{\pi})=R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}) . The fundamental question we ask is: Within the sample-and-evaluate framework, how many samples from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} are necessary and sufficient to achieve low regret with respect to a given comparator policy π ⋆ \pi^{\star} and how should we select which output to return? In order to answer this question, we have to better understand in what sense the reward model r ^ \widehat{r} is close to the true reward r ⋆ r^{\star} and in what sense the reference policy π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is a good proxy for the comparator policy π ⋆ \pi^{\star} . We discuss these two questions in turn below.

sections.heading: 2.2 In what sense is r ^ \widehat{r} close to r ⋆ r^{\star} ?
sections.text: Our first goal is to formalize the sense in which the learned reward model r ^ \widehat{r} is close to the true reward r ⋆ r^{\star} . Critically, the reward model r ^ \widehat{r} is trained on ‘typical’ outputs, which we formalize by assuming that r ^ \widehat{r} is close to r ⋆ r^{\star} on samples drawn from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} . While Huang et al. [14] supposed that the squared error , ε RM 2 ​ ( r ^ ) = 𝔼 y ∼ π ref ​ [ ( r ^ ​ ( y ) − r ⋆ ​ ( y ) ) 2 ] \varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\left[\left(\widehat{r}(y)-r^{\star}(y)\right)^{2}\right] is small, we argue that this is not the most appropriate metric in our setting for two reasons. First, squared error is not scale-invariant , i.e., multiplying r ^ \widehat{r} by a positive constant does not change the behavior of any selection algorithm that uses r ^ \widehat{r} to select outputs, but it does change the squared error. Second, assuming small squared error is somewhat unnatural when rewards are only accessible through pairwise comparisons. Indeed, there is a philosophical point to be made here: if rewards are only accessible through pairwise comparisons, then it is not clear that there is any meaningful ground-truth numerical reward function r ⋆ r^{\star} at all beyond the ordinal information it induces. Numerical reward functions are often trained by running Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) on pairwise comparison data assuming the Bradley-Terry model [ 4 , 27 ] , which is known to suffer sample complexity scaling exponentially in the maximum reward value 3 3 3 Indeed, it arises naturally as a simple calculation reveals that the maximum inverse Fisher information scales similarly. [ 28 , 35 ] . Instead, we propose to measure the quality of r ^ \widehat{r} through its pairwise win-rate error with respect to r ⋆ r^{\star} : ε pw ( r ^ ) := 𝔼 y , y ′ ∼ π ref [ | ϕ r ^ ( y , y ′ ) − ϕ r ⋆ ( y , y ′ ) | ] and ϕ r ( y , y ′ ) := 𝟏 { r ( y ) > r ( y ′ ) } + 1 2 1 { r ( y ) = r ( y ′ ) } \displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}):=\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}\!\left[|\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})|\right]\quad\text{and}\quad\phi_{r}(y,y^{\prime}):=\mathbf{1}\{r(y)>r(y^{\prime})\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}\{r(y)=r(y^{\prime})\} (3) Here, ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) quantifies the amount by which r ^ \widehat{r} disagrees with r ⋆ r^{\star} on the outcome of two ‘typical’ responses sampled from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} . In particular, the absolute difference | ϕ r ^ ​ ( y , y ′ ) − ϕ r ⋆ ​ ( y , y ′ ) | |\phi_{\widehat{r}}(y,y^{\prime})-\phi_{r^{\star}}(y,y^{\prime})| vanishes when r ^ \widehat{r} and r ⋆ r^{\star} agree on the pairwise comparison outcome between y y and y ′ y^{\prime} , is 1 / 2 \nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} when one of the reward functions has a tie and the other does not, and penalizes disagreements between r ^ \widehat{r} and r ⋆ r^{\star} that flip the win-versus-loss outcome with a full penalty of 1 1 . This definition of ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) is thus closely aligned wth the notion of win rate, which rewards strict wins more than ties. This alignment with the win-rate functional (which also half-counts ties and ranges between 0 0 and 1 1 ) hearkens back to our discussion on win-rate in Section 1 and will prove to be important in our later analyses. This metric is clearly scale-invariant and more closely matches the way reward models are trained in practice [ 24 , 27 , 19 ] , suggesting that ( 3 ) may be a more reasonable quantity to expect controlled than ε RM 2 \varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}} . In the Bradley-Terry model, an elementary analysis shows that the tightest relationship between the two quantities scales exponentially in the maximum reward value, suggesting that when learning with finitely many samples from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , we may expect ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) ≪ ε RM 2 ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\ll\varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r}) . In general, however, ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) is incomparable to ε RM 2 ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r}) as we show in Appendix A . Indeed, the scale invariance of ε pw \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}} immediately implies that there are examples where ε pw = 0 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}=0 but ε RM 2 \varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}} is arbitrary. Another sense in which requiring ε RM 2 ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon^{2}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{RM}}(\widehat{r}) to be small is a stronger assumption than requiring ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) to be small is that we cannot recover small regret in terms of expected true reward from small ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) (cf. Proposition 3 in Appendix A ), in marked contrast to small ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r}) [ 14 ] ; as we discussed above, in many situations, winrate is the more natural notion of reward.

The first term quantifies the degree to which reward hacking occurs: as N N increases, the algorithm is more likely to select outputs on which r ^ \widehat{r} and r ⋆ r^{\star} disagree. The second term quantifies the extent to which, even if r ^ = r ⋆ \widehat{r}=r^{\star} , the BoN algorithm is able to find high-reward outputs comparable to those of the comparator π ⋆ \pi^{\star} using only samples from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} ; here the ℰ N \mathcal{E}_{N} -divergence naturally arises as the relevant measure of discrepancy between π ⋆ \pi^{\star} and π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} due to the connection between ℰ N \mathcal{E}_{N} and approximate rejection sampling outlined in Block and Polyanskiy [2] . [14] , although we emphasize that here we are considering win rate as opposed to expected reward. In the special case of binary rewards, however, expected reward becomes a special case of win rate (cf. Section 2 ), and thus the above upper bound recovers the result of Huang et al. [14] in this setting. In contradistinction to the case of expected reward, where BoN’s performance is suboptimal statistically, we find that BoN is in fact optimal for win-rate regret up to constant factors, as established by the following lower bound.

sections.heading: Theorem 4 .
sections.text: For any non-atomic π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , any π ^ 𝒜 \widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{A}} in the sample-and-evaluate framework, and any ε < 1 / 2 \varepsilon , there exist reward functions r ^ \widehat{r} , r ⋆ r^{\star} satisfying ε pw ​ ( r ^ ) ≤ ε \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}(\widehat{r})\leq\varepsilon and a comparator policy π ⋆ ≪ π ref \pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} for which R r ⋆ ( π ⋆ ) − R r ⋆ ( π ^ 𝒜 ) ≳ inf M { M ⋅ ε + ℰ M ( π ⋆ ∥ π ref ) } . \displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathcal{A}})\gtrsim\inf_{M}\left\{M\cdot\varepsilon+\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})\right\}. (9) This result shows that unlike in the expected-reward setting, BoN is in fact optimal up to a logarithmic factor for win-rate regret within the sample-and-evaluate framework, which helps explain its widespread practical use despite its simplicity. This observation gently pushes back against the conclusion reached by Huang et al. [14] that observed that, when optimizing for expected reward, BoN is statistically suboptimal and more sophisticated algorithms are necessary to achieve optimal performance. As we have emphasized repeatedly, however, we believe that win rate is often a more natural objective than expected reward in many practical settings, and thus the suggestion that BoN should be avoided for being statistically suboptimal may be overstated. In addition to the statistical lower bound above, we also provide a complementary computational lower bound.

sections.heading: Proposition 1 .
sections.text: For any M ≥ 2 M\geq 2 and δ < 1 / 2 \delta , there exist reward functions r ⋆ = r ^ r^{\star}=\widehat{r} and policies π ⋆ , π ref \pi^{\star},\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} with ℰ M ( π ⋆ ∥ π ref ) = 0 \mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=0 such that within the sample-and-evaluate framework, any policy π ^ \widehat{\pi} achieving regret R r ⋆ ​ ( π ⋆ ) − R r ⋆ ​ ( π ^ ) ≤ δ R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi})\leq\delta must use at least N = Ω ~ ​ ( M ) N=\widetilde{\Omega}(M) samples from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} . This bound is computational in the sense that if we did not care about computational efficiency (quantified by N N in the sample-and-evaluate framework), then it is trivial to achieve small regret with π ^ BoN \widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} , as r ^ = r ⋆ \widehat{r}=r^{\star} ; on the other hand, if we want to achieve small regret, then we have a strong lower bound on the number of samples required. We emphasize that this lower bound matches the upper bound of Theorem 3 and thus BoN is computationally and statistically optimal for win-rate regret within the sample-and-evaluate framework.

sections.heading: 4 Achieving Optimal Performance without Reward-Hacking
sections.text: While in the previous section we saw that the naïve Best-of- N N algorithm given in ( 7 ) is computationally and statistically optimal for win-rate regret with optimally tuned N N , it is still susceptible to reward-hacking. That is, as N N increases, the algorithm is more likely to select outputs on which r ^ \widehat{r} and r ⋆ r^{\star} disagree, leading to performance that scales non-monotonically in N N . While understandable, this is an unfortunate property, as in practice one would like to be able to increase N N to improve performance without worrying about overfitting to the reward proxy r ^ \widehat{r} . In this section, we present a new algorithm, ℰ M \mathcal{E}_{M} -regularized Best-of- N N , that is able to mitigate reward-hacking and achieve performance that is monotone in N N while still being statistically and computationally optimal. Intuitively, we would like a policy that returns high-reward outputs without straying too far from the reference policy π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , as outputs that are unlikely under π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} are more likely to be subject to reward-hacking. Our analysis and results from the previous section suggest that the appropriate way to measure discrepancy from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is via the ℰ M \mathcal{E}_{M} -divergence for an appropriate choice of M M , defined in ( 4 ). Motivated by this observation, we consider the following variational problem: π M ∈ argmax π 𝔼 π [ r ^ ( y ) ] − R max ⋅ ℰ M ( π ∥ π ref ) , \displaystyle\pi_{M}\in\argmax_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\widehat{r}(y)\right]-R_{\mathrm{max}}\cdot\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), (10) whose solution we refer to as the ℰ M \mathcal{E}_{M} -regularized Best-of- N N policy . Note that it is perhaps not immediate that ( 10 ) is a desirable objective to consider; indeed, while a similar objective, with ℰ M \mathcal{E}_{M} replaced by χ 2 \chi^{2} , was considered by Huang et al. [14] in the context of expected reward maximization, in our setting we do not care about the expected reward per se, but rather the win-rate. Another potential concern is that the variational problem in ( 10 ) is not easily sampled from within the sample-and-evaluate framework, as it is not immediately clear how to draw samples from the optimal policy π M \pi_{M} . The second concern is allayed, however, by the following result, which shows that the optimal policy for ( 10 ) takes a particularly simple form.

sections.text: One might instead consider a different variation of ( 10 ), where R max R_{\mathrm{max}} is replaced by a general scaling parameter β > 0 \beta>0 . sections.heading: Theorem 5 .
sections.text: For any M , N ≥ 1 M,N\geq 1 , reference model π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , comparator π ⋆ ≪ π ref \pi^{\star}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , ground truth reward r ⋆ r^{\star} , and learned reward model r ^ \widehat{r} , it holds that R r ⋆ ( π ⋆ ) − R r ⋆ ( π ^ M ) ≲ ℰ M ( π ⋆ ∥ π ref ) + M ⋅ ε pw + 1 N , \displaystyle R^{r^{\star}}(\pi^{\star})-R^{r^{\star}}(\widehat{\pi}_{M})\lesssim\mathcal{E}_{M}(\pi^{\star}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})+M\cdot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pw}}+\frac{1}{N}, (11) Note that the upper bound in ( 11 ) is very similar to that of BoN in Theorem 3 , with the key difference being that the scaling parameter N N is now decoupled from the regularization parameter M M . As a result, by tuning M M appropriately, we can achieve the performance skyline established in Theorem 3 while maintaining monotonicity in N N . Other than monotonicity, the monotone algorithm performs similarly to BoN and we note that it still requires tuning of the regularization parameter M M , so we expect BoN to remain the dominant alignment algorithm when monotonicity is not required. We conclude this section by observing that the only prior provably monotone algorithm, the χ 2 \chi^{2} -regularized Best-of- N N algorithm proposed by Huang et al. [14] , can fail to achieve optimal performance when win-rate regret is the goal. Specifically, we have the following result.

sections.heading: 5.1 Proof Sketch of Theorem 3
sections.text: In order to compare the performance of π ^ BoN \widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{BoN}} to that of an arbitrary comparator policy π ⋆ \pi^{\star} under the true reward function r ⋆ r^{\star} , we need to overcome two main challenges: (1) if N N is too small and π ⋆ \pi^{\star} is far from π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} , then we could pay in regret for not being able to find high-reward outputs comparable to those of π ⋆ \pi^{\star} ; and (2) if N N is too large, then we may overoptimize r ^ \widehat{r} and select outputs on which r ^ \widehat{r} and r ⋆ r^{\star} disagree. sections.heading: 7 Discussion and Related Work
sections.text: In this work, we studied the problem of inference-time alignment within the sample-and-evaluate framework, focusing on the widely used Best-of- N N (BoN) algorithm. In contradistinction to prior work that focused on expected true reward as the objective of interest, we argued that win rate is often a more natural objective in practical settings where reward models are trained and evaluated using pairwise comparisons. We demonstrated that BoN is both statistically and computationally optimal within the sample-and-evaluate framework for achieving good win rate, partially explaining its widespread practical success despite its simplicity. Because BoN remains susceptible to reward-hacking even under the win-rate objective, we proposed a simple variant that provably eliminates reward-hacking while maintaining optimal statistical performance. Our work suggests several interesting directions for future research. First, we may ask if there is a unifying paradigm that captures both expected-reward and win-rate objectives as special cases, allowing us to better understand under what conditions (optimally tuned) BoN is optimal and when more sophisticated algorithms are necessary. Second, while we have focused on the sample-and-evaluate framework as a natural abstraction of inference-time alignment, it would be interesting to understand if similar statistical and computational guarantees can be achieved in more general frameworks that allow for adaptive sampling or other forms of interaction with the reference model. Finally, while our proposed variant of BoN eliminates reward-hacking in theory, it may still be too conservative in practice due to its reliance on information-theoretic guarantees; moving beyond such guarantees and leveraging the rich structure that learned representations provide in order to improve inference-time alignment remains an interesting question. We now discuss several related works in more detail.
